books.section: Topic 4.3 Politics and Regional Interests, C. A Temporary Truce on the Slavery Question in the Pre-Civil War Period

stimulus.text:
Thomas Jefferson, retired at Monticello, wrote to Congressman John Holmes about the Missouri question on April 22, 1820:

“but this momentous question, like a fire bell in the night, awakened and filled me with terror. I considered it at once as the knell of the Union. it is hushed indeed for the moment. but this is a reprieve only, not a final sentence. a geographical line, coinciding with a marked principle, moral and political, once conceived and held up to the angry passions of men, will never be obliterated; and every new irritation will mark it deeper and deeper.”
stimulus.source_note: Thomas Jefferson to John Holmes, April 22, 1820; text verified against Founders Online and the Library of Congress. Public domain.

source: original; stimulus is a verbatim excerpt from Jefferson to John Holmes, April 22, 1820 (public domain, verified against Founders Online)
stem: When Jefferson writes that the Missouri question “is hushed indeed for the moment,” he most likely means that

options.text: Congress had voted to stop debating slavery forever
options.misconception: No vote ended debate on slavery; the gag rule that tried to came sixteen years later, and it failed.

options.text: the Compromise had quieted the debate without settling the question
the public had lost interest in the Missouri question
options.misconception: Jefferson says the question filled him with terror; lost interest fits neither his tone nor the letter.

options.text: Jefferson himself had stopped following public affairs
options.misconception: Jefferson says he had stopped reading newspapers, yet this very letter shows him following the Missouri fight closely.

rationales.A: Nothing in 1820 ended debate on slavery. The House tried to silence it with the gag rule in 1836, and that only made the fight louder.
rationales.B: “Hushed for the moment” plus “a reprieve only, not a final sentence” means quiet now, unsettled underneath. The Compromise paused the fight; it did not end it.
rationales.C: A question that wakes a man “like a fire bell in the night” has not lost the public’s interest. Jefferson’s terror is the opposite of indifference.
rationales.D: Jefferson does say he had stopped reading newspapers, but he writes this letter because the Missouri question broke through that retirement. Following it is the point of the letter.
rationales.general:
1. Read the sentence whole. “Hushed indeed for the moment” has a qualifier in it: for the moment.
2. Read the next sentence. “A reprieve only, not a final sentence” says the quiet is temporary by design.
3. Ask what a reprieve is. A delay of a sentence, not a pardon. The question is still waiting.
4. Put it together. Jefferson is saying the Compromise bought quiet, not peace.
Background: the Missouri Compromise passed in March 1820, a month before this letter, admitting Missouri as a slave state and Maine as a free state.
Remember: “for the moment” is a time limit, so ask what happens when the moment ends.
